Mobile Portfolio Strategy · Tier A Diagnostic & Predictive Review

Where to build next on Google Play — and how much of the answer this catalog can actually give

A category-entry and reach-banding review of 9,659 Play Store listings, after correcting two field-level errors that invalidate the standard analysis.

Prepared for the Head of Mobile Product · Source: Google Play Store catalog scrape, vintage August 2018 · 58 statistical tests, 8 reach models, 8 rating models · Path A (diagnostic) + Path B (predictive); Path C (causal) out of scope

Executive Summary

Situation

A studio choosing its next build needs to know which Play Store categories are crowded, which sustain paid distribution, and what reach a new listing can realistically expect. This 9,659-app catalog snapshot is the most widely used public dataset for exactly that question.

Complication

Two of its headline fields do not mean what published analyses assume. Rating is missing for 15.1% of apps because Google withholds it below a review threshold - those apps have a median of 1 review and 100 installs - so every 'average rating by category' figure is a survivor statistic. And Reviews, the feature most notebooks feed to install models, reproduces 91% of install variance on its own.

Resolution

Corrected, the catalog still answers the entry question - but differently than expected. Crowding is not the constraint (HHI 0.0727); monetization structure is (PERSONALIZATION 21.5% paid vs 0% in three categories). Pre-launch reach is forecastable at macro-F1 0.503 against a 0.132 baseline - enough to band a portfolio, not to pick winners (26% blockbuster recall). Rating is unforecastable (R-squared 0.074 against a pre-registered 0.15 bar).

Enter on monetization structure rather than crowding, band expected reach with a model that must never be used to pick winners, and drop app rating from the greenlight scorecard entirely - it cannot be forecast, and the field itself is censored.

  1. The catalog's quality metric is structurally censored. 15.1% of apps carry no rating, and 91.8% of those sit in the under-1,000-install tier. Dropping them - the standard move - removes the long tail and turns every category-quality comparison into a survivor statistic.
  2. Crowding is not the entry constraint; monetization structure is. At HHI 0.0727 the catalog is unconcentrated, but paid viability runs from 21.5% in PERSONALIZATION to 0% in three categories, with confidence intervals clear of the 7.77% average.
  3. Reach travels with maintenance and payload, not with quality. Days-since-update (-0.33) and app size (+0.31) are the strongest listing associations; category explains just 2.6% of rating variance. All are associations, not causes.
  4. Reach is forecastable pre-launch; rating is not. A tuned model reaches macro-F1 0.503 (3.8x baseline) on decade-scale tiers - but finds only 26% of blockbusters, capping it to banding. 8 models missed the pre-registered rating bar.
Recommendation — who does what, by when

Mobile Product selects the target category on paid-share and reach-distribution evidence - not on crowding - at the next build review.

Mobile Product adopts the reach model for budget banding only, with per-category error monitoring, and explicitly bars it from greenlight selection.

Mobile Product removes app-rating forecasts from the greenlight scorecard before the next cycle, and re-scopes rating to a post-launch monitoring metric.

15.1%of apps have no rating — median 1 review
0.0727HHI — the catalog is unconcentrated
0.503reach macro-F1 vs 0.132 baseline
0.074rating R² vs a 0.15 pre-set bar

So whatThe 1,463 apps without a rating are not missing data to be dropped - they are the smallest apps in the store, and they are absent by design. Every 'average rating by category' figure published from this dataset silently conditions on apps that survived long enough to be rated.

ImplicationRating statistics must carry their denominator, and Rating cannot be imputed - imputation would fabricate exactly the tail that is missing.

Part I · Diagnostic

What the catalog measures, and what it actually shows

Key Line 1 · Branch A The quality metric is structurally censored, so the standard analysis measures survivors

Google does not publish a star rating until an app accumulates reviews. That single product decision makes Rating missing-not-at-random in the strongest possible sense: the missingness is generated by the outcome. The consequence is that 1,463 apps — the smallest in the catalog — vanish from every rating statistic ever computed on this dataset.

So whatThe rated subsample has a median of 100,000 installs; the unrated one has 100. These are two different populations, not one population with holes in it.

ImplicationAny category-quality comparison built on rated apps only describes incumbents. It cannot tell a studio what a NEW listing should expect.

So whatThe obvious challenge to Key Line 1 is that small apps simply have thinner metadata. If that were true, every optional field would thin out together. They do not: 'Varies with device' RISES with scale while Rating missingness FALLS.

ImplicationThe finding survives its most likely objection, so the rating denominator is a real correction rather than an artifact of data quality.

Key Line 2 · Branch B Crowding is not the entry constraint — monetization structure is

The intuition that the store is saturated does not survive measurement. What does separate categories is whether they sustain paid distribution at all, and that varies by more than twenty percentage points with confidence intervals that do not overlap.

So whatFAMILY leads at 19.6%, and HHI 0.0727 sits far below the 0.15 'unconcentrated' threshold. The intuition that the store is dominated by a few categories is not supported.

ImplicationCategory choice should not be driven by avoiding crowded categories. The differentiating factor is monetization structure (EX 5), not headcount.

So whatAgainst a 7.77% catalog average, PERSONALIZATION (21.5%) and MEDICAL (20.7%) run above 20%, while HOUSE_AND_HOME, BEAUTY, COMICS sustain none. The confidence intervals do not overlap the average, so this is structure, not sampling noise.

ImplicationChoose the monetization model WITH the category, not after it. A paid launch into a 0%-paid category bets against every incumbent's revealed pricing.

So whatThe mean-to-median gap is 4.7x, created entirely by the 'I Am Rich' family of joke apps. They are real listings and are retained; the statistic is changed instead.

ImplicationPrice a new paid app in the $0.99-$4.99 band where 75% of paid listings sit. Never quote a mean price from this catalog.

So what81.6% of the catalog is rated "Everyone", but DATING sits at 9% and SOCIAL and ENTERTAINMENT below 40%. Audience access is set at category level.

ImplicationA category whose norm is Teen-or-above carries a reach ceiling no listing optimisation removes. Factor it into the addressable-market estimate before committing.

Part II · Predictive

What can be forecast before launch — and what cannot

Key Line 3 · Branch C Reach travels with maintenance and payload; quality explains almost nothing

No single listing attribute explains much of reach on its own, which is precisely the case where a multivariate model earns its place. Rating, by contrast, is a near-constant: compressed into half a star and censored on top of that.

So whatBlockbusters are a median 40 MB and updated within a fortnight; niche apps are ~8 MB and six months stale. No other listing attribute comes close to these two.

ImplicationASSOCIATION, NOT CAUSE. Popular apps can afford maintenance, so causality plausibly runs backwards. 'Update more often to grow' is not supported by this data and is not recommended.

So whatThe target is both compressed (SD 0.536 stars, 70% inside a 0.7-star band) and censored (EX 1). Even the winning model explains under 8% of what little variance exists.

ImplicationRemove rating forecasts from the greenlight scorecard. Rating is an outcome to monitor after launch, not a variable to plan with.

Key Line 4 · Branch D Reach is forecastable at decade resolution — enough to band a portfolio, not to pick winners

Two things had to be fixed before a model could be trusted: the leakage that inflates every published result on this dataset, and the target specification that makes reach look unlearnable. With both corrected, the model is genuinely useful — and its single most important property is a limitation.

So whatWith Reviews the model scores R-squared 0.939; without it, 0.423. Reviews only exists after launch, so it cannot inform a pre-launch decision at all.

ImplicationPublished notebooks reporting ~0.9 on this dataset are measuring the outcome against itself. Every model in this report excludes Reviews and its derivatives.

So whatAt the raw 20-bracket resolution the same features reach macro-F1 0.098 - the model names the modal bracket and nothing else. Collapsed to four decade-tiers it becomes genuinely useful.

ImplicationForecast reach as an order of magnitude, never as an install count. The install field is a bucket floor, so precision beyond a decade is not available in principle.

So whatAggregate performance is real, but 323 of 437 top-tier apps are missed, almost all mistaken for the tier below. The model cannot see what separates a hit from a solid performer.

ImplicationUse the model to BAND expected reach for budgeting. Do NOT use it to select which app to greenlight - it would reject three-quarters of the eventual hits.

So whatUnder-prediction averages 20.8% but varies widely by category. A model used to allocate budget would give systematically conservative estimates to the categories at the high end.

ImplicationMonitor per-category error rates in production and manually review the high-under-prediction categories. Otherwise the model quietly entrenches existing category size.

Appendix

Methodology, limitations and audit trail

A1 · Data lineage and grain

Source: googleplaystore.csv (10,841 × 13), SHA-256 recorded at ingestion; raw data never edited. One corrupted row (left-shifted fields) was dropped after a right-shift repair was attempted and rejected — it leaves Category, the primary analytical dimension, unrecoverable.

Two grains are maintained, not one. Repeated app names have two unrelated causes: re-scrape repetition (a defect, collapsed by keeping max reviews) and genuine Play Store cross-listing — 85 apps hold two real categories, because FAMILY is an overlay rather than a peer of GAME. Market-structure statistics therefore run on the (App, Category) grain (9,744) and models on the App grain (9,659). Every exhibit states which it used.

Denominator note, because the grain moves the headline figure. Apps missing a rating are 1,474 of 10,840 raw rows (13.6%) but 1,463 of 9,659 unique apps (15.1%). The two differ because re-scraped duplicates skew toward larger, already-rated apps, so collapsing to one row per app raises the missing rate. This report quotes the app-grain figure throughout, since the question concerns apps rather than scrape rows. Both are correct; neither appears without its denominator.

A2 · The censoring test and its control

Three tests establish that Rating is not observed at random: 100% missingness among zero-review apps; monotone decay across all 21 install brackets (Cochran–Armitage z = -58.6); and a Cliff's delta of 0.885 between the install distributions of rated and unrated apps.

The control is what makes the claim defensible. The obvious objection is that small apps simply carry thinner metadata. If so, other optional fields would thin out the same way. They do the opposite: rating missingness correlates -0.55 with install tier while "Varies with device" correlates +0.32 (Size) and +0.29 (Android version). The censoring is specific to the field.

A3 · Statistical discipline

At n = 9,659 a Cohen's d of 0.06 clears p < 0.05, so effect sizes lead every claim and p-values appear only in tables. Wilson intervals on every proportion (the normal approximation fails at the 0% and 100% cells this data contains); Benjamini–Hochberg FDR within each test family; Holm correction within the 33-category paid-share family. Every "no meaningful effect" claim ships with its minimum detectable effect at 80% power. Non-parametric companions (Kruskal–Wallis, Mann–Whitney) accompany parametric tests because ratings are skewed −1.75, and they agree.

Worked example of the trap: paid apps rate 0.18 SD higher than free apps at p < 0.001 — but that is 0.10 stars on a five-point scale, against an MDE of 0.12. Reported as significant-but-trivial rather than as a finding.

A4 · Leakage control

Reviews and every derivative, all install aliases, Rating, and Rating_Observed are banned from pre-launch models. Rating_Observed is the subtle one: the censoring result makes it a near-deterministic function of install tier, i.e. a disguised label. The ban is asserted programmatically against the fitted transformer's output feature names, not merely intended. Reviews_per_Install — suggested by the source data review — was never created: it is a ratio of a leak to a bucket floor.

A5 · The pre-registered rating falsification

Written into the notebook before any rating model ran: "We accept Rating as a usable greenlight-scorecard target if any model achieves 5-fold CV R² ≥ 0.15 using pre-launch features only." The bar was set deliberately low — roughly a quarter of the rating's own standard deviation — so a rejection could not be blamed on a demanding threshold. 8 families were built and tuned. Best achieved: R² 0.074. Verdict: REJECT.

A6 · Model specification

Stratified 5-fold CV, seed 42 throughout. Random splitting is correct here and the reason is stated rather than assumed: this is a cross-sectional snapshot with no time index, and the near-duplicate risk that would demand grouped CV was removed by collapsing to the app grain. All encoding, imputation and scaling live inside a Pipeline, fit on training folds only. Two baselines throughout (majority and stratified). Primary metric is macro-F1; accuracy appears once, attached to the majority baseline, to retire it. Model artifact and card: models/model_card.json.

A7 · Fairness

A protected-subgroup audit is impossible and that impossibility is a finding, not an omission: the data describes apps, not people, and contains no demographic, user, or developer attribute. This caps any deployment recommendation.

Two audits are runnable and were run. Per-category error rates (Exhibit 13) matter because a model that informs budget allocation and systematically under-bands certain categories would entrench their size. Per-tier recall (Exhibit 12) is the blockbuster limitation. Category and primary genre also proxy for publisher scale and business model, and are flagged as such in the model card.

A8 · Monitoring plan — specification only, not validated here

PSI on feature distributions and on predicted-tier mix against the training snapshot; retraining trigger at macro-F1 below 0.40 on a freshly labelled monthly sample. The expected failure mode is vintage drift: a 2018 catalog's size norms and Android version floors do not describe today's store. Nothing in this plan is tested on this data, and it is labelled accordingly.

A9 · Limitations

  • Survivorship, and it is not fixable. Only apps live at scrape time are present. Delisted and failed apps are absent, so every "successful category" statistic partly reflects which failures were removed. No modelling recovers this.
  • Installs is a bucket floor, never a count. The field holds 21 ordinal brackets; every install figure here is a lower bound and is labelled as one. No mean of bucket labels is ever computed — the single most common misuse of this dataset.
  • Rating describes established apps only. Per Key Line 1, all rating statistics carry the 8,196-app denominator.
  • The snapshot is August 2018 (max Last Updated), not "early 2019" as the source documentation states — that is the publication date. The reach model is period-specific by construction.
  • No causal claim is available. There is no time dimension, no intervention and no assignment mechanism. Path C was declared out of scope at framing, and every driver in this report is labelled an association.
  • No revenue, retention, developer identity, region, or review text. Monetization findings stop at list price and say nothing about earnings.
  • The reach model must not select. 26% blockbuster recall means it would reject roughly three-quarters of eventual hits.

A10 · Reproducibility

  • Six notebooks, restart-and-run-all clean, seed 42 throughout
  • Raw source hashed (SHA-256) and never edited; cleaning log records every action and three deliberate non-actions
  • Every number in this report is read from reports/_key_figures.json — the report hardcodes no statistic
  • Dependencies pinned in requirements.txt
  • Self-contained HTML: inline CSS, base64 figures, zero external requests
